one_liner: Pure-Rust WebRTC/RTP/SRTP stack with its own ICE, DTLS and SCTP; first-party data-channel loopback runs 3.3x webrtc-rs and 3.2x pion.
what_it_does: A tokio-based real-time communication library: one PeerConnection type covers WebRTC (ICE, DTLS, SRTP, SCTP data channels), plain RTP and SRTP, and, behind the t38 feature, a T.38 fax terminal, with RTP packetizers, jitter buffer, NACK/RTX, TWCC/GCC bandwidth estimation, TURN, ICE-TCP, mDNS and UPnP. The API follows the W3C shape (create_offer, set_local_description, create_data_channel, add_track) but is its own Rust interface, so moving from webrtc-rs or pion means rewriting call sites; data-channel events arrive through an async recv() queue instead of callbacks. There is no C API.
how_it_is_fast: It replaces webrtc-rs's layered crates with in-tree implementations: an SCTP association (src/transports/sctp.rs) that drains up to 1000 queued chunks per transmit pass under one lock, delivers the next in-order TSN straight to the channel without touching the reassembly queue, sends SACKs with SACK_DELAY = 0 and computes the CRC-32C checksum with SSE4.2 or the aarch64 CRC instructions; a homegrown DTLS 1.2 record layer using RustCrypto AES-128-GCM; Bytes buffers and parking_lot locks; and fat LTO with one codegen unit in the release profile. Part of the published gap comes from the benchmark configuration rather than the stack: rustrtc's default data channel is reliable unordered (DataChannelConfig derives Default, so ordered = false and DATA chunks carry the U flag), while both baselines run ordered reliable channels.
when_to_use: Rust SIP/WebRTC gateways, SFUs or voice-agent backends (the author's rustpbx and active-call) that need ICE, DTLS-SRTP, RTP and data channels in one dependency without OpenSSL or libwebrtc.
Many concurrent peer connections in one process where memory matters: 21 MB peak RSS for ten loopback pairs against 44 MB for webrtc-rs and 48 MB for pion in the author's run.
Bulk data-channel transfer where message order does not matter, which is exactly the default rustrtc channel and the case the benchmark measures.
Mixed telephony deployments that also need plain RTP latching, RTP rewrite bridging, UPnP port mapping or T.38 fax alongside WebRTC.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ applications: there is no C ABI; libwebrtc or libdatachannel are the native options, and neither was compared.

Expecting the 3.3x on ordered channels: every quoted throughput number compares rustrtc's unordered channel with ordered channels in webrtc-rs 0.17.1 and pion v3.3.6, so no like-for-like ordered result exists; ordered receive also caps pending out-of-order messages per stream at 128 (MAX_INBOUND_STREAM_PENDING).

Deployments that need an audited TLS stack: DTLS handshake and record layer are written in-house (src/transports/dtls), and the ClientHello also offers TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, a suite without forward secrecy, after the two ECDHE suites.
CPU-bound hosts: in the same run rustrtc used 739.62% CPU against 555.20% for pion, so the gain is in throughput per CPU-percent (0.74 against 0.31 MB/s), not lower absolute CPU.
Code that needs a frozen API: 0.3.x has had 145 patch releases since 2025-11-27 and still ships protocol-behaviour fixes (two ICE restart/nomination issues, #54 and #55, open on 2026-10-04).

integration.dependencies: tokio (multi-thread runtime), RustCrypto aes/aes-gcm/ctr/hmac/sha1/sha2/md-5/p256, rcgen (ring) and x509-parser for certificates, bytes, parking_lot, socket2, crc32fast/crc32c, igd (UPnP), serde/serde_json, tracing, rand, base64, local-ip-address
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2024 with let-chains in src (Rust 1.88 or later); no rust-version is declared; the README run used rustc 1.97.1
integration.platforms: Any tokio target; hardware CRC-32C on x86-64 (SSE4.2) and aarch64 (CRC extension), software fallback elsewhere. The benchmark ran only on Linux x86-64.
integration.thread_safety: PeerConnection and DataChannel are shared through Arc and used from multiple tokio tasks (the benchmark spawns sender and receiver tasks per pair); sends on one channel serialise on a per-channel async lock. A tokio runtime is required.

gotchas: create_data_channel(label, None) gives a reliable unordered channel, unlike the W3C, webrtc-rs and pion default of ordered; pass a DataChannelConfig with ordered = true if the application relies on order.

Data-channel events go into an unbounded tokio mpsc queue, so a slow consumer grows memory instead of exerting SCTP backpressure. On the send side, send_data waits once flight plus queued bytes exceed sctp_max_buffered_amount (256 KB by default).

The benchmark's 'Setup Latency' is not comparable across stacks: the rustrtc arm starts its timer only after both peers report Connected and then reads a DataChannelEvent::Open that may already sit in that queue, while the webrtc-rs and pion arms start after pc1 alone is Connected and wait for an on_open callback; pion's figure is also truncated to whole milliseconds.

The harness's send-side pacing differs per stack: rustrtc's send_data has the built-in 256 KB limit, the pion sender blocks above a 100 KB bufferedAmount threshold, and the webrtc-rs sender has no explicit gate. CPU is the process-lifetime ps %cpu value, sampled every 500 ms in Rust and every 2000 ms in Go, from one run per stack.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The only transport sibling is uvgRTP, a C++ RTP library for high-rate media without ICE, DTLS or data channels; pick rustrtc when a Rust service needs a full WebRTC peer (ICE, DTLS-SRTP, SCTP data channels) and pick uvgRTP for raw RTP streaming from C++. The codec siblings (opus-rs from the same author, dav1d, the Opus ports) solve a different problem and pair with it rather than compete.
verified_claims_summary: Author's single run at release 0.3.141 on an Intel i7-9700T (8 cores, Debian 13), rustc 1.97.1 with fat LTO for rustrtc and webrtc-rs 0.17.1 in one example binary, go 1.24.4 for pion v3.3.6: ten in-process loopback pairs each push 1 KiB messages for 10 s, giving 549.04 MiB/s for rustrtc against 165.98 (webrtc-rs) and 169.58 (pion). The comparison is not like-for-like: rustrtc's channel is unordered while both baselines are ordered, the stacks pace their senders differently, and the setup-latency timers start at different points, so the 3.3x figure is an upper bound for unordered bulk transfer, not a general WebRTC speedup.
status_note: Very active (352 commits, 0.3.145 published 2026-10-03, issues closed within days) and MIT-licensed, so it is easy to adopt in Rust, but its speed evidence is first-party, it is networking rather than audio or video coding, and its security-critical DTLS is homegrown.
